A making-of · November 2026

Making Mulberry Bush

How a 1976 shadow dance became a three-minute film of four lanterns circling a bush that grows because they dance around it. Every image and every sound was generated by code.

This report follows the order the work happened in: watching the original, choosing an idea, building the pieces, fixing what looked wrong, delivering the film, and then rebuilding it as a web page that makes the film as you watch.

At a glance

What was made

Mulberry Bush (2026): a round for four dancers. 3:00, 1080 × 1080, 30 fps, stereo. It is the same square frame and almost the same length as the 2:54 original.

Saved as Mulberry Bush 2026 (master).mp4 (895 MB) and a share copy (108 MB) in the project folder. The master was also copied to My Drive/generated videos/. The code that makes it is four Python files, listed at the end.

There is also a live version: a 379 KB web page that draws and plays the film in the browser, on GitHub Pages.

Step 1

Watching the original

I can't play a video the way a person does. I watch a film by turning it into contact sheets: one frame every two seconds, tiled into grids with timestamps, which I then look at as images. Four sheets covered the 2:54 film.

What I took from it:

  • Four dancers in a side view, often joined hand to hand in a chain or ring.
  • The film's real subject is how a dancing figure can be drawn: it keeps changing the rendering style while the dance continues.
  • The light is behind the screen and the figures are shadows on it. The film continues what the audience had just seen live, which was your shadows on the backlit screen.

For the sound I took the audio track's frequency spectrum every six seconds. The strongest peaks sat on C, D, E and G (262, 294, 330, 392 Hz and their octaves), and the beat repeated about every half second. So it is continuous music in C major, at roughly 120 beats a minute. I measured this only so I could make the new score clearly different.

Step 2

Finding the idea

You asked for a radical reinterpretation that keeps the Mulberry Bush concept, with no tracing. Before writing any code I listed directions and tested each against two questions. Does it keep the round dance around a bush? Is it a real change of point of view, rather than the old film redrawn?

  • keptTurn the piece inside out. In 1976 the light was behind the dancers and the dancers were shadows. Make the dancers the light, and let the bush cast the shadows. Look down from above instead of from the side.
  • keptThe dance grows the bush. Plants bend toward light. If the four lanterns circle, the shoots chase them and the bush grows in a spiral, so the dance leaves a record in the plant.
  • keptA round is a round. A ring dance and a musical round (a canon) share a name. Four dancers become four voices entering one after another.
  • folded inSilk. Mulberry leaves feed silkworms. This became the lantern trails in the weaving section, threads wound around the bush.
  • folded inThe rhyme's week of chores. Day after day became season after season: one year in one night, ending at sunrise.
  • folded inFootprints as dance notation. The dancers' bodies are never drawn. Only their feet are, as dew prints and later as mulberry-juice prints, the way old dance-step diagrams record a dance.
  • droppedThe bush's point of view (camera at the centre looking out). Strong, but it hides the circle, which is the thing the dance makes.
  • droppedPlanets and orbits. Pretty, but it turns dancers into physics.
19762026

The performance shaped one more decision. In 1976 the film sat between two live dances. So the new film starts with four lights walking in from the four corners, as if the dancers had stepped into the screen. It ends with each one walking out of the corner it came in by, one at a time, which cues the live dancers to return.

Step 3

One clock for picture and sound

Picture and sound are made by separate programs, so they need one shared clock. I measured the film in bars of 6/8 instead of seconds. A bar normally lasts 1.5 s. It shrinks to 0.8 s during the whirlwind (an accelerando), stretches for the night and dawn, and a single 2.2-second bar holds the moment everything stops. Every motion and every note is placed in bars and converted to seconds through the same table. That keeps the footsteps on the beat even while the tempo changes.

Section widths are drawn to scale in seconds. A lap of the ring normally takes 8 bars (12 s); in the whirlwind it falls to about 3 s.

Step 4

The film, section by section

Step 5

How the pieces work

The bush is grown, not drawn

Seven shoots start at the centre when the dancers have joined hands. Every 1/30 of a second each growing tip turns a little toward the lanterns (nearer ones pull harder), a little outward, and a little counter-clockwise, plus some randomness. Every 15–28 px a tip splits in two.

A coarse grid records which shoot has passed where, and a tip that runs into a different shoot stops. That keeps the bush airy instead of tangled. Branch thickness comes from how many tips grow beyond a segment, so trunks are thick and twigs are fine.

Because the lanterns move counter-clockwise while the bush grows, the result is a pinwheel. A different dance would grow a different bush.

Light and shadow

Each lantern is a point light carried above head height. For every pixel of ground the renderer adds up the four lanterns' light, with brightness falling off with distance. Each lantern is also aimed slightly toward the bush, the way someone holding a lamp faces what they circle. For shadows, every branch, leaf and berry is projected away from each lantern onto the ground, drawn into four soft masks, and each mask removes only that lantern's colour. A spot shaded from the rose lantern is still lit by teal, violet and gold, so its shadow has colour.

At dawn a fifth light, the sun, casts parallel shadows that start almost horizontal and shorten as it rises.

Dancing in footprints

Footprints are placed on the music: in 6/8 a skip is step-hop, step-hop, so the prints land on eighth notes 0, 2, 3 and 5 of each bar, left-left-right-right. In the whirlwind they switch to running (every eighth). At night they switch to walking. Dew prints fade after seven seconds. After the berries fall, the prints are mulberry juice and stay.

The weave

When two dancers reverse, they must pass each other alternately inside and outside the ring, like a maypole. Each opposite-direction pair gets a fixed sign. Because every dancer meets its two oncoming partners in turn, its sign flips at each meeting.

for a in (0, 2):              # dancers still going counter-clockwise
    for b in (1, 3):          # dancers going clockwise
        s = +1 if (a + b) % 4 == 1 else -1
        bump = gaussian(angle_between(a, b))   # only near a meeting
        radius[a] += 50 * s * bump
        radius[b] -= 50 * s * bump

The sound

The tune is eight bars. It opens with the traditional mulberry-bush figure (do-do-do-do-mi, sol-sol-mi-do), and the rest is new. It uses only the five notes G A B D E, so any two bars can sound together over a drone. That is what lets it work as a four-part round with each voice two bars behind the last. The four instruments are built from sine waves:

  • Rose lantern: plucked string, harmonics that die away faster the higher they are.
  • Teal lantern: flute, with vibrato and breath noise.
  • Violet lantern: reed, odd harmonics strong like a clarinet.
  • Gold lantern: marimba, a struck bar with its characteristic overtone near four times the pitch.

Each note is panned to wherever its dancer is on screen at that moment, so with headphones you hear the four go round. While two dancers go backwards, their voices sing the tune backwards (in retrograde). Other sounds come from the same simulation:

  • a soft thump for every one of the 1,392 footprints;
  • a music-box note for each new shoot;
  • a glass note as some berries redden, and a plop as each one bursts;
  • wind that grows with the dancers' speed;
  • crickets at night and birds at dawn.

A drone shifts from G to E (minor) for the fruit, to C for the whirlwind, and back to G for morning.

Step 6

What looked wrong, and what I changed

I work by rendering a handful of stills from across the film, looking at them, and changing one thing at a time. There were about eight rounds of this before the full render.

The bush that wouldn't branch

The first growth run produced seven bare stems and nothing else. The cause: when a tip split, the new shoot marked its starting cell on the grid. On the very next step the parent was still in that cell, saw a different owner, and stopped itself. Letting a shoot pass through cells owned by its own parent or children fixed it, and the count went from 352 segments to about 5,000.

From fog to night

Getting there took three swings. A physically correct falloff made the pools tight but left the bush in darkness, so its shadows were invisible. A softer falloff brought the haze back. Aiming each lantern slightly toward the bush resolved it: bright where the action is, dark outside the ring.

The sunrise shadow

I first modelled the bush as a dome, highest in the middle. At sunrise that cast a strange detached fan of shadow. A real shrub rises from its base like a vase. Once the centre was at ground level, the morning shadow started at the base and fanned out long and soft.

Smaller fixes

  • Ripe berries showed as bubblegum pink, so I deepened them toward dark red and near-black.
  • Footprints were too small to read as feet, so I made them 30% bigger.
  • The flying autumn leaves looked like confetti dots, so they now grow as they rise toward the camera and carry a midrib.
  • The dawn ground was washed out to beige, so I lowered the sky light and warmed the sun.
  • In the soundtrack, the rustle of unfurling leaves was an 18-second wall of hiss; it now comes in gusts. The footsteps were too busy, and night and dawn were 9 dB quieter than the rest, so I lowered the footsteps and raised night and dawn.

ffmpeg wasn't installed. I found two copies on the machine. One came with CEWE Creator, but that is a 2019 build that can only encode with OpenH264. The other was in another Claude session's scratch folder. I didn't use that one, because you had asked me not to look at other versions, and its folder was part of one. I installed a fresh build instead.

The render ran as eight parallel processes. Each drew its share of the 5,394 frames and piped them straight into its own x264 encoder, so no frames were stored as images. The eight pieces were then joined without re-encoding. A frame took about 1.3 seconds alone, and about 3.5 seconds each when all eight processes shared the CPU. The soundtrack took about four minutes to synthesise.

Step 9

Limits, plainly

  • I haven't heard the soundtrack. Levels, balance and the spectrogram look right, but timbre and mix are untested by ear.
  • The coloured shadows are subtler than I intended. They show best in the bare-bush sections and get lost under the full canopy.
  • At small sizes the footprints read as dashes. At full size they are clearly feet.
  • The master is large (895 MB) because the per-frame film grain is costly to compress. The share copy smooths it slightly.
Step 10

The film as a web page

After the film was finished, you asked whether a web page could generate the same film at the same quality. My answer was yes for everything the programs decide, and no for anything left to chance. So the page isn't sent the video. It is sent the decisions: the grown bush, every footprint, every note. Then it does the drawing and the synthesis itself. That is how a three-minute 1080 × 1080 film fits in a 379 KB page.

Ship the decisions, not the pixels

Two exports carry everything the Python programs decided:

  • The world. All 5,005 branch segments, in the order render.py draws them, plus the leaves, berries, juice stains, footprints and dew glints. Each column is stored as 16-bit integers, which keeps positions to about a hundredth of a pixel.
  • The score. Instead of rewriting the composition logic, I ran audio.py itself with its instruments wrapped, so that each sound was written down instead of mixed. The random-number stream advanced exactly as in the real render. The 3,413 recorded events are the same notes, footsteps, tinks, plops, crickets and birds, at the same times, volumes and stereo positions.

Packed and compressed, both come to 208 KB. The 5.9 MB ground texture couldn't come along, because claude.ai refuses pages well under 1 MB. So the page regrows it in a background thread from the same recipe of soil, moss, grass blades and pebbles. With different random numbers the moss lands in different places, so I tried 24 seeds and kept the one whose colour around the bush is closest to the original.

Drawing it on the graphics card

Each frame, the page works out the same state render.py does: how far every shoot has grown, how wide it is, its colour under the four lanterns, and where its shadow falls from each one. That comes to about 45,000 small shapes. The graphics card draws them into layers: the marks on the ground, the bush, the light trails, and four shadow masks. It blurs the masks and the glow, then computes the lighting for each of the 1.17 million pixels. A frame takes 10 to 16 ms, well inside the 33 ms a 30 fps film allows.

Composing the sound in the page

I ported the four instruments and the bells, plops, footsteps and birds, then checked each one against its Python version. All of them matched to within 0.06 dB, and the drone and the wind matched exactly. The first full run took 14.5 seconds on one processor core. In the browser, the built-in reverb then took another 13 seconds, because it has to run the whole three minutes through a 3.2-second room.

So the page splits the timeline between up to six background workers, balanced by how much work each stretch of the score is. Each worker synthesises its stretch and adds the room itself, using a fast Fourier transform. The page then adds the pieces together, which works because reverb is linear, and applies the final fade and limiter. The soundtrack is now ready in about six to nine seconds.

Pressing play doesn't wait for it. The film starts on the computer's clock. As soon as the sound is ready, it takes over as the clock, without a jump.

Checking it against the film

I pulled frames from the master MP4 with ffmpeg and had the page render the same moments. I compared them in two ways: numerically, as the average colour of 81 squares per frame, and by eye in magnified crops. In the final version the average difference per square is 1 to 3 levels out of 255 in every section. Where the bush and the prints are, the closest match is at zero offset: the shapes sit on the same pixels.

What the comparison caught

  • Too green. The first regrown ground was 3 levels too green everywhere. The moss patches are so large that how much of the frame they cover varies a lot from seed to seed, hence the seed search.
  • Faint footprints. The prints at night and the dew prints looked washed out next to the film. My first theory was wrong: the change it suggested made the dew prints fainter still. Reading how Pillow draws settled it. On a transparent layer, Pillow doesn't blend; it overwrites colour and alpha together, and the 2× downsampling then darkens soft edges. The page now draws those layers into two targets, one for colour and one for alpha, both written in proportion to how much of each pixel a shape covers. That reproduces the film's darker prints and the thin dark edge along every branch.
  • Soft leaves. Leaves and feet are drawn from small stencil images. For long, thin shapes the graphics card picked too blurred a version of the stencil, until I turned on anisotropic filtering.
  • Credits that pop. In the film, the credits switch on at full brightness instead of fading in. For the same Pillow reason, the fade I had written into render.py was ignored. Measuring the MP4 frame by frame confirmed it. I kept the pop in the page, because the brief was the same film.
  • Lettering. Windows' Garamond can't be served on the web. EB Garamond came out about 35% heavier. Cormorant Garamond sets "Mulberry Bush" within a pixel of the original width, at nearly the same weight.
  • Credits that seemed to be missing. At 2:55 neither version showed the last two credit lines, which looked like a bug in both. It wasn't one: I had miscounted the film as 116 bars instead of 115, and those lines appear half a second later.

The browser pane in this app was hidden for most of the work. A hidden page runs in the background: it doesn't draw animation frames, its screenshots go stale, and its timings are slowed. So I had the page send its comparison images to a tiny local server that saved them to disk, and looked at them there. I tested playback by advancing the player's clock by hand.

The player

The page is a plain film player in the film's colours. A strip under the picture shows the ten sections to scale, and you can click or drag along it. Beside the time are the bar number and six beat dots, in two groups of three, lit on each eighth note of the 6/8 bar. There are volume, mute and full-screen controls. Keys: space plays, the arrows skip and change the volume, M mutes, F fills the screen. Your browser remembers the volume.

Where it is

  • GitHub Pages, public: toontalk.github.io/mulberry-bush-2026, from the repository ToonTalk/mulberry-bush-2026, which also holds the source code under the MIT licence.
  • claude.ai, private until you share it: the same page as an artifact.
  • On disk: Mulberry Bush 2026 (live).html in the project folder. It opens straight from disk, with no server.

Limits of the web version

  • I haven't heard this soundtrack either. It matches the Python mix to within 0.5 dB in every section. The reverb is a fresh random room, so each note's ring differs slightly from the film's.
  • I checked the finished player by measuring its layout, at desktop and phone widths, not by seeing it on screen. The pane was hidden.
  • It is untested on real phones. Phones get three sound workers instead of six to save memory, but their frame rate is unknown.
